strengths: The paper offers a useful architectural contribution: differentiable subpixel primitive placement combined with entropy-based density allocation and learned multi-view confidence. Although its components build on established techniques, their integration addresses a practical limitation of feed-forward Gaussian reconstruction.

The quality–primitive-count tradeoff is well supported. In Table 3, the full method uses 38,400 primitives per image versus 268,324 for the full-resolution pixel baseline, while improving SSIM from 0.5695 to 0.5998 and LPIPS from 0.3597 to 0.3379 at similar PSNR. This is valuable independently of benchmark leadership.

Table 1 shows consistent PSNR and SSIM improvements over the evaluated baselines on DL3DV across all four view counts. At three views, the method achieves 20.12 dB versus 18.61 for VGGT+DepthSplat and 17.64 for AnySplat. Qualitative comparisons also demonstrate sharper details and fewer visible primitive artifacts.

Rendering-based fine-tuning improves camera-pose estimation over pretrained VGGT across all tested Charge configurations: AUC@15 increases from 0.8011 to 0.8476 with 25 views. The paper additionally measures depth and intrinsics, providing a useful assessment beyond rendering alone.

The combined evidence favors weak acceptance: compact representations, improved perceptual quality, and consistent pose gains constitute a supported contribution, despite reservations about attribution, reproducibility, and broader claims.
weaknesses: The ablations do not cleanly isolate continuous placement from adaptive allocation. Table 3 changes both when comparing the full method with pixel-aligned baselines; without adaptive density, detection performs worse than both pixel baselines on all three rendering metrics. A matched-budget comparison that changes only center placement is needed to substantiate the specific causal claim about going off the grid.

Novel-view evaluation mixes reconstruction quality with method-dependent target-pose estimation. Target images enter a separate N+T forward pass for pose recovery, while FLARE uses target-view optimization that reportedly fails. This protocol is disclosed and does not feed target images into Gaussian construction, but it limits conclusions about rendering quality alone and weakens the FLARE comparison.

The broad state-of-the-art and geometry-improvement claims exceed the results. On sparse Charge settings, VGGT+DepthSplat has higher PSNR and SSIM; AnySplat has better LPIPS at 6, 9, and 25 views. Depth accuracy is worse than pretrained VGGT at every tested view count, and Charge focal-angle accuracy also deteriorates. The evidence supports pose improvements and a favorable compactness tradeoff, rather than uniformly improved geometry or rendering.

Reproducibility is materially limited despite the supplementary architecture details. The manuscript omits optimizer settings, learning rates, training duration, loss weights, Gaussian scale bounds, and precise training-subset composition. These omissions are particularly consequential because the paper explicitly reports instability without teacher regularization.

There are correctable but substantive inconsistencies in the method specification. The density percentages sum to 105%. The stated opacity penalty sin(alpha*c) is monotonically increasing on [0,1], so minimizing it favors zero rather than both binary endpoints. Equation 1 also uses the primitive-count symbol P as the spatial summation bound. These issues leave the implemented allocation and objective uncertain.

Efficiency is demonstrated through primitive counts, without measured inference latency, rendering throughput, or peak inference memory. The decoder overhead and large VGGT backbone mean that fewer primitives alone do not establish the claimed end-to-end speed or scalability advantages.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful problem: reducing redundant primitives in feed-forward Gaussian reconstruction. Combining differentiable subpixel placement, entropy-based density allocation, and confidence-based aggregation provides a coherent alternative to dense pixel-aligned decoding.

Table 3 supports a meaningful quality–compactness improvement for the complete method: 38,400 primitives per image achieve 19.09 PSNR, 0.5998 SSIM, and 0.3379 LPIPS, compared with 19.02, 0.5695, and 0.3597 for the 268,324-primitive pixel-aligned baseline. The contribution therefore has value beyond benchmark ranking.

Evaluation covers real and synthetic scenes and multiple input-view counts. On DL3DV, the method obtains the best reported PSNR and SSIM at every evaluated view count. Figures 6–8 provide qualitative support for sharper details and fewer structured artifacts.

Rendering-based fine-tuning consistently improves camera-pose AUC over pretrained VGGT on Charge: AUC@15 increases from 0.7599 to 0.7887 with three views and from 0.8011 to 0.8476 with 25 views. This is a useful empirical finding, even though improvements do not extend uniformly to other geometry outputs.
weaknesses: The ablations establish the complete system's benefit more clearly than the central claim about off-grid placement. In Table 3, detection without adaptive density performs worse than both pixel-aligned baselines on all three image-quality metrics. The full comparison changes both placement and density allocation; there is no matched-budget fixed-location control isolating continuous placement. Consequently, attributing the gains specifically to escaping the pixel grid remains insufficiently supported.

Novel-view evaluation conflates rendering quality with target-pose estimation. Section 4.1 uses the target RGB images in a separate forward pass to estimate their cameras, with different alignment procedures across methods. This does not mean target images construct the evaluated Gaussian model, but it makes the results dependent on method-specific registration accuracy. The reported FLARE alignment failures particularly weaken that comparison, and no common-pose evaluation separates these effects.

Reproducibility is materially incomplete. Neither the main text nor the supplied supplement specifies the combined loss weights, optimizer, learning-rate schedule, training duration, precise training subsets, or Gaussian scale bounds. There are also concrete specification errors: the density allocations sum to 105%, and the stated opacity penalty sin(alpha × confidence) is monotonically increasing on [0,1], so minimizing it favors zero rather than both binary endpoints. The latter contradicts its stated purpose; its effect cannot be assessed without the actual implementation and loss weight.

The efficiency evidence consists primarily of primitive counts. No measured inference latency, rendering throughput, or peak-memory comparison substantiates the broader speed and scalability claims. This matters because the system retains a large VGGT backbone and adds decoding computations; fewer output primitives do not by themselves establish faster reconstruction.

The broad state-of-the-art and geometry-improvement claims need qualification. On Charge, VGGT+DepthSplat has better PSNR and SSIM in every sparse configuration, while AnySplat has better LPIPS at 6, 9, and 25 views. Depth accuracy is consistently worse than pretrained VGGT in Table 2, and Charge focal-length angular metrics also deteriorate. Overall, the supported compactness and rendering improvements are substantial, but incomplete attribution, evaluation confounds, and missing training specifications place the manuscript near the acceptance boundary.

strengths: The paper makes a useful contribution to feed-forward 3D Gaussian reconstruction: differentiable subpixel primitive detection, entropy-based density allocation, and confidence-based aggregation offer a practical alternative to dense pixel-aligned decoding. Although the components build on established techniques, their integration addresses a meaningful representation-efficiency problem.

The quality–primitive-count tradeoff is supported quantitatively. In Table 3, the full model uses 38,400 primitives per image versus 268,324 for the full-resolution pixel baseline, while improving SSIM from 0.5695 to 0.5998 and LPIPS from 0.3597 to 0.3379 at essentially equal PSNR. This is valuable independently of benchmark leadership.

Table 1 shows consistent PSNR and SSIM improvements over the evaluated baselines across all four DL3DV settings. For three views, the method achieves 20.12 dB versus 18.61 for VGGT+DepthSplat and 17.64 for AnySplat, with substantially fewer primitives. Qualitative comparisons also illustrate sharper detail and reduced grid artifacts.

Rendering-based fine-tuning improves camera-pose accuracy over pretrained VGGT across all four Charge configurations in Table 2. Ablations establish that adaptive density and learned confidence materially improve the complete system. Together, these results support weak acceptance, despite limitations in attribution, reproducibility, and the breadth of the claims.
weaknesses: The ablations do not cleanly isolate the benefit of subpixel placement. The full model changes both placement and density allocation relative to the pixel baselines, while fixed-density detection performs worse than those baselines on all three reported image-quality metrics. A matched-budget, matched-density comparison with fixed centers or direct coordinate regression is missing. The evidence therefore supports the combined decoder more strongly than the claim that leaving the grid itself causes the improvement.

Novel-view evaluation conflates rendering quality with target-camera estimation. Section 4.1 estimates target poses using a second forward pass containing target images; this does not directly feed target appearance into the Gaussian reconstruction, but makes the evaluation conditional on target-image-assisted localization. Alignment also differs across methods, and FLARE demonstrably fails to align. These results establish practical pipeline performance more clearly than an isolated rendering advantage.

The strongest performance and geometry claims exceed the results. On Charge, VGGT+DepthSplat has higher PSNR and SSIM in all sparse settings, and AnySplat has better LPIPS at 6, 9, and 25 views. Depth accuracy is worse than pretrained VGGT in every Table 2 setting, and Charge focal-length angular metrics also deteriorate. The supported conclusion is improved pose estimation and competitive rendering with fewer primitives, rather than uniformly improved geometry or state-of-the-art performance.

Important reproducibility details are absent even from the supplement: the combined loss and its weights, optimizer, learning-rate schedule, training duration, precise dataset subsets and mixture, and Gaussian scale bounds. There are also consequential specification inconsistencies: density percentages sum to 105%, and the stated opacity penalty sin(αc) is strictly increasing on [0,1], so it favors zero rather than both binary endpoints as claimed. These may be correctable errors, but the actual implemented training objective cannot be recovered confidently from the manuscript.

Efficiency is demonstrated through primitive counts rather than measured runtime or memory. No reconstruction latency, rendering throughput, or peak-memory comparison substantiates the claims of generation within seconds and improved computational efficiency. The counts also do not clearly distinguish allocated primitives from those retained after confidence pruning.

strengths: The paper offers a useful contribution to feed-forward 3D reconstruction: a differentiable, patchwise Gaussian placement decoder combining continuous coordinates, adaptive density, and confidence-based aggregation. Although its ingredients are established, their integration addresses a meaningful quality-versus-representation-size problem.

Table 1 provides substantial evidence across six diverse datasets. Average PSNR improves from 17.71 for AnySplat and 18.83 for DA3 to 21.21, while using 0.1431 Gaussians per input pixel versus 0.8141 and 1, respectively. The combination of better rendering and substantially fewer primitives is practically valuable.

The internal comparisons support the proposed design beyond comparisons with external models. Table 3 improves average PSNR by 0.30 dB and reduces LPIPS from 0.4341 to 0.3796 relative to pixel-aligned prediction; the offset baseline performs worse. Table 4 also supports adaptive density and confidence weighting.

Geometry evaluation and qualitative results complement the rendering metrics. Table 2 shows improved average depth, pose, and intrinsics estimates over the pretrained VGGT backbone, while Figures 6–8 illustrate sharper reconstructions and fewer artifacts. Together, these results favor acceptance despite the methodological and reproducibility reservations below.
weaknesses: The opacity regularizer is technically inconsistent with its stated purpose. Section 3.3 minimizes sin(alpha*c), but alpha*c lies in [0,1], where sine is strictly increasing. Thus, this term favors zero opacity rather than both zero and one. Since the paper attributes reduced half-transparency partly to this regularizer, the discrepancy affects interpretation of the method, rather than merely presentation.

The evaluation measures rendering together with method-dependent camera estimation. Target images enter a second forward pass to estimate target poses, and alignment assumes that context-only and context-plus-target predictions differ only by scale. Target appearance does not directly construct the Gaussian model, but pose errors can influence the reported rendering differences. The substantial geometry differences in Table 2 make it difficult to attribute the full Table 1 gains specifically to primitive placement.

Reproducibility is incomplete even with the supplement: optimizer settings, training duration, learning rates, loss weights, Gaussian scale bounds, and precise training subsets are missing. The density allocation percentages sum to 105%, leaving the actual allocation ambiguous. Tables 3 and 4 also report different full-model results from Table 1 without clearly identifying the corresponding configuration changes.

The ablations do not fully isolate the proposed allocation mechanism. Table 3 changes both placement and primitive count without a matched-budget fixed-placement baseline; Table 4 omits primitive counts for its variants. Consequently, the evidence supports the combined decoder more strongly than a specific explanation based on continuous placement or entropy allocation alone. The teacher losses and opacity regularizer also lack direct ablations.

Efficiency claims extend beyond the measurements provided. Primitive-count reduction is demonstrated, but reconstruction latency, rendering throughput, peak memory, and scaling with view count are not reported. The claimed generation in seconds and potential for higher-resolution processing therefore remain insufficiently quantified.

strengths: The paper presents a useful contribution to feed-forward 3D reconstruction: patch-local, continuous Gaussian placement combined with adaptive primitive allocation and confidence-based aggregation. Although the components build on established techniques, their integration addresses a meaningful limitation of dense pixel-aligned representations.

Table 1 supports a strong quality–compactness tradeoff across six datasets. Average PSNR improves from 17.71 for AnySplat and 18.83 for DA3 to 21.21, while using 0.1431 Gaussians per input pixel versus 0.8141 and 1, respectively. The method leads in PSNR and SSIM on every evaluated dataset; the qualitative comparisons also show clearer structures and reduced artifacts.

The internal comparisons provide evidence beyond comparisons between independently trained systems. Table 3 improves average PSNR from 18.33 to 18.63 and LPIPS from 0.4341 to 0.3796 over the pixel-aligned variant. Table 4 additionally supports the usefulness of adaptive density and confidence.

The geometry evaluation and supplementary depth visualizations help characterize the effects of photometric fine-tuning. Overall, the supported reconstruction and compactness benefits favor acceptance, although the methodological ambiguities and incomplete experimental controls below prevent a stronger recommendation.
weaknesses: The stated opacity regularizer does not have its claimed behavior. Section 3.3 minimizes sin(alpha*c), with alpha*c in [0,1]. This function is strictly increasing on that interval, so minimization favors zero opacity, rather than both zero and one. Because this regularizer is explicitly credited with addressing transparency artifacts, the discrepancy affects the technical explanation, not merely presentation.

Important reproduction details are missing even from the supplement: loss weights, optimizer, learning rates, training duration, dataset subset sizes and mixture weights, and Gaussian scale bounds. The density allocation is also inconsistent: 55% low, 35% medium, and 15% high sum to 105%. Equation 1 incorrectly uses the primitive count P as the spatial summation bound. The latter appears to be a notation error, but the allocation rule leaves an actual implementation choice unresolved.

The evaluation measures reconstruction together with method-dependent target-camera estimation. Target RGB images enter a separate context-plus-target forward pass, and alignment assumes that the two predictions differ only by scale. The paper acknowledges this consistency assumption but does not quantify its error. This does not demonstrate target-image leakage into Gaussian construction, but it makes the large cross-method NVS gains difficult to attribute specifically to primitive placement rather than camera and intrinsic accuracy.

The ablations do not fully isolate the source of improvement. Table 3 compares against a much denser pixel-aligned representation without a matched-primitive-budget control. Table 4 does not report primitive counts or clearly distinguish removing confidence weighting from removing the final pruning threshold. Furthermore, full-model scores differ between Tables 1, 3, and 4 without explaining the evaluation or training differences. These omissions limit conclusions about which mechanisms drive the gains.

Efficiency is demonstrated through primitive counts, not measured end-to-end performance: inference latency, rendering throughput, peak inference memory, and scaling with resolution or view count are absent. Thus the compactness claim is supported, while claims about generation speed and scalability remain less established. Some performance wording is also too broad: DA3 has better MipNeRF360 LPIPS in Table 1, and the proposed method does not improve every geometry metric over VGGT in Table 2.

strengths: The paper makes a useful contribution to feed-forward 3DGS: differentiable sub-pixel primitive placement, entropy-based density allocation, and confidence-based fusion provide a practical alternative to dense pixel-aligned prediction. The originality lies in this decoder design and its integration, rather than in the individual established components.

Table 1 provides substantial evidence across six datasets: average PSNR improves to 21.21 dB versus 17.71 for AnySplat and 18.83 for DA3, while using 0.1431 Gaussians per input pixel versus 0.8141 and 1. This quality–compactness improvement has clear practical value.

The controlled comparisons support the proposed design. Table 3 reports a 0.30 dB improvement and approximately 13% lower LPIPS over the pixel-aligned variant; Table 4 supports adaptive density and confidence. Qualitative examples also show sharper details and reduced structured artifacts.

Geometry evaluation complements rendering metrics: Table 2 shows improved average depth, pose, and intrinsics estimates over the initial VGGT backbone. Together with the decoder ablations and broad evaluation, the supported contribution favors acceptance despite the reservations below.
weaknesses: The opacity regularizer is mathematically inconsistent with its stated purpose. Section 3.3 minimizes sin(alpha*c), but this function is strictly increasing for alpha*c in [0,1], encouraging zero rather than both binary endpoints. This is consequential because the paper attributes reduced half-transparency to this loss; the reported formulation does not establish that explanation.

The evaluation measures reconstruction and camera estimation jointly. Target images enter a second forward pass to estimate evaluation cameras, and scale-only alignment assumes consistency between predictions from different view sets. This disclosed protocol does not directly contaminate the context-only Gaussian model, but method-dependent camera errors confound attribution of the large gains to primitive placement. Common-camera or controlled-geometry comparisons would strengthen that attribution.

Reproduction is hindered by missing optimizer settings, learning rates, training duration, loss weights, exact training subsets, and Gaussian scale bounds, including in the supplied supplement. The density percentages also sum to 105%, leaving the actual allocation ambiguous. These omissions affect implementation beyond editorial polish.

The compactness evidence is stronger than the computational-efficiency evidence. No measured inference latency, rendering throughput, peak memory, or scaling curves substantiate the claims of reconstruction in seconds or improved scalability; fewer output Gaussians do not establish lower end-to-end cost for the VGGT-based pipeline.

The ablations do not fully isolate placement from primitive budget and adaptive allocation, and their evaluation settings are insufficiently explained despite differing full-model scores from Table 1. The claim of superiority on all metrics is also overstated: DA3 has better MipNeRF360 LPIPS, and better average depth and pose metrics in Table 2.
